accuracy.evidence: Every pair was checked against the National Curriculum in England English Appendix 1 Years 3-4 homophone list (brake/break, grate/great, meat/meet, peace/piece, plain/plane, heel/heal, rain/rein/reign, here/hear) and the Year 2 list for there/their/they're. The /eɪ/ spellings ei (vein, veil, rein), eigh (eight, weigh, sleigh, neighbour) and ey (they, grey, obey, prey) come from the same appendix. Meanings were checked against the Oxford Children's Dictionary: brake is the stopping device, grate is to shred or a fireplace grate, plain is simple or flat land. Near-homophones (accept/except) are named as near, not identical.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented Key Stage 2 errors: choosing by sound alone (step 1 feedback 'break sounds right, but look at the meaning', mend step 'Press the break'), their for 'there is' (mend line 3, challenge 'place2'), forgetting the they're contraction (swap-test feedback 'they are fits, so write they're'), letter swaps in learned spellings (challenge 'peice', mastery 'peece'), phonetic spellings of /eɪ/ (prediction 'thay', challenge 'ayt' and 'braik', p5 'Thay') and confusing homophones with rhymes or synonyms (challenge 'rhyme' and 'same', m1).

lab_distinct.evidence: flaghphone is built around meaning choosing between two spellings of one sound: a picture sentence accepts only the spelling that matches the picture, a gap card is sorted by grammatical role with the they-are swap test, and a mnemonic step lights only the clue letters inside the word (ear in hear, pie in piece, here in there). flagaltsp teaches graphemes for a phoneme and flagtgraph counts trigraph phonemes; neither asks the meaning to decide. The lab_distinct gate passed under the 30% similarity limit.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child acts first and the text confirms: the bike picture rejects break with the two meanings shown side by side, the there/their/they're box refuses a wrong card and offers the swap test in the sentence itself, the clue step lights e-a-r in hear only when all three are tapped, and the ay builder refuses 'thay'-style choices by naming the word family (they, grey, obey). Every completion line restates the meaning rule just used.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions each carry a tempting wrong option that the lab then disproves: 'Yes, they sound the same' for brake/break (disproved when only brake fits the bike sentence), 'There' for '___ coats are wet' (disproved in the sort when their is the only accepted box) and 'thay' for they (disproved when only ey completes th_).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Eleven distinct wrong-answer messages keyed to the slip: here as a place word (place), heer not a word (spell), their as ownership (own), there as place (place2), peace as calm (calm), the swapped peice (ie), ate as the past of eat (ay8), braik as a sound-it-out spelling (ayk), break as smash (smash), same-spelling confusion (same) and rhyme versus homophone (rhyme). Six questions rotate, so a retry gives a new item.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences and everyday words, one idea each (what a homophone is, think about meaning, clues inside words, there/their/they're, the ay spellings); the validator's family readability limit passed. Lab prompts are a few words on big tiles. The adult text uses the precise terms homophone, near-homophone, contraction, grapheme and the /eɪ/ phoneme.

no_filler.evidence: No warm-up sentences; the content gate found no banned phrases and explanation overlap stayed under 12% against every lesson, including Alternative Spellings for Sounds, which mentions here/hear in passing. Each feedback line gives the two meanings or the clue, for example 'peace means calm. A part of a cake is a piece, like a piece of pie.'

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 screenshots for all 6 steps: the bike picture, dashed gap and two choice tiles stack vertically and fit 390 px; the three there/their/they're boxes share the width with readable 19 px labels; the hear letter tiles are about 60 px; the ay builder gap and ei/eigh/ey keys are large; the mend sentence shrinks to one line. A row of full-size buttons under the canvas repeats every action.

accessibility.evidence: The walkthrough gate completed every task with Show me on desktop and iPhone 13, and axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) reported no violations in light or dark. Every drag or tap has a labelled button (e.g. 'Put brake in the gap', 'The gap is they're', 'Use eigh'), and the canvas aria-label is rewritten with each feedback message so a screen reader hears the result.

sources: National Curriculum in England: English programmes of study, English Appendix 1 Spelling, Years 3 and 4 (homophones and near-homophones; /eɪ/ spelt ei, eigh, ey) and Year 2 (there/their/they're)
